REFERENCE DATA FOR UCL HPC

refdata-flow

Checked, versioned reference data for every analysis on Myriad, Kathleen and Young.

Nicholas Owen · UCL Advanced Research Computing · November 2026

Thanks for having me. I’m Nicholas, from ARC. This is refdata-flow, a pipeline for a problem that quietly costs all of us time: getting hold of clean, versioned reference data, and the files that go with it. It has changed a lot since I last showed it. It has grown from genomes and annotations to the derived files, variant resources and databases our analyses actually use, and it is getting ready to run on the UCL clusters. I’ll cover what it is, how it works, and why it is worth using across UCL HPC.

THE PROBLEM

Every analysis starts with a download

Somebody downloads a genome. Then somebody else downloads it again.

The same FASTA fetched again and again on one shared filesystem.

Groups quietly running against different Ensembl releases.

“Where did this come from?” answered from someone’s bash history.

A resource that says chr1 beside a genome that says 1, and the analysis runs to the end anyway.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Every analysis begins with reference data: a genome, an annotation, and increasingly a pile of things beside them, such as known-sites files, a VEP cache or a protein database. Almost every project starts the same way. Someone finds a download link and puts the file in a scratch directory; the next person can’t find it, so they download it again. Different groups end up on different releases. The provenance is whatever is in someone’s bash history. The last one is the nastiest: a resource that names its chromosomes chr1, beside a genome that names them 1. Nothing fails. The tools simply match nothing, and the analysis runs to the end.

OVERVIEW

One CSV in, a checked vault out

A Nextflow pipeline that turns a short list of species queries into a checked, versioned, refgenie-managed reference vault.

INPUT

A CSV of queries

GRCh38 · mouse · sacCer3

ENGINE

Nextflow and genomepy

conda · resume · parallel

OUTPUT

A refgenie vault

digest · aliases · RO-Crate

CONSUMED BY

Paths from refgenie seek

rnaseq-flow · GATK · VEP

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

In one sentence: a Nextflow pipeline that takes a small CSV of species queries and produces a checked, versioned, refgenie-managed reference vault. You write what you want in plain terms: GRCh38, mouse, sacCer3. The pipeline works out what that means, downloads it from the right provider, checks it, and files it under a digest of its sequences. Tools consume it through explicit paths: you ask refgenie seek for human/fasta and get a path you can hand to anything. It is the upstream sibling of rnaseq-flow: same Nextflow style, same conda profile, same SGE profile.

HOW IT WORKS

Four stages, one command

01 · Resolve

02 · Fetch

03 · Register

04 · Derive and check

Plain queries become exact assemblies. Ambiguity is asked once, and mistakes are caught before any download.

resolve.py

A preflight asks the vault first. Only what it lacks is downloaded, four at a time, retried on failure.

genomepy

Each genome is filed under a digest of its sequences, with a sequence dictionary and your aliases.

refgenie 0.13

Derived files are made from the vault; third-party resources are checked against their genome.

gffread · UCSC · htslib

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Under the hood there are four stages, and the last three now run inside one Nextflow run. A Python resolver turns generic queries into exact assemblies, asking you when a query matches more than one, and caching the answer. It also catches three mistakes before anything downloads: an annotation asked for where none is published, two rows that are really one download, and one alias given to two genomes. Nextflow then fetches, but only after a preflight asks the vault what it already holds. Registration files each genome under its digest, adds a sequence dictionary so the FASTA works with GATK and Picard as it is, and links your aliases. Finally the pipeline derives the files analyses ask for, and fetches and checks the third-party resources you requested. Each stage restarts safely on its own.

WHAT LANDS IN THE VAULT

One vault, five kinds of data

KindWhat it holdsRead by
GenomesFASTA with .fai, .dict and chrom sizesaligners, GATK, Picard
AnnotationsEnsembl, GENCODE, UCSC or NCBI GTF, tagged by releasequantifiers, aligners
Derived filestranscriptome, tx2gene, indexed GTF, BED12, refFlat, 2bitsalmon, tximport, VEP, RSeQC, Picard, deepTools
ResourcesClinVar, ENCODE blacklist, GATK bundle, dbSNP, VEP cacheGATK, VEP, filtering
DatabasesSwiss-Prot, Pfam, SILVA, Kraken 2, filed beside the vaultsearch and classification tools

No aligner indexes: they depend on a tool version and k-mer choices, which belong to an analysis.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

This is what a run leaves you with. Genomes, each with an index, a sequence dictionary and chromosome sizes beside the FASTA. Annotations from the same provider as the genome, each tagged with its release. The small derived files every project used to regenerate slightly differently: a transcriptome cut from the vault’s own genome and GTF with gffread, tx2gene, an indexed GTF, BED12, refFlat and a 2bit, each tagged with the annotation it came from. Third-party resources asked for by name and build: ClinVar, the ENCODE blacklist, the six GATK known-sites files, dbSNP and the VEP cache. And databases that belong to no genome, such as Swiss-Prot, Pfam, SILVA and Kraken 2 indexes, filed by name and version beside the vault. Deliberately, no aligner indexes: those depend on the tool version and choices like k-mer size, which belong to an analysis, not to a reference.

WHY RUN IT ON UCL HPC

What it gives researchers on the clusters

One copy, the same release for everyone, mistakes caught early, and a record for every file.

So far, what it is. Now why it matters on the UCL clusters specifically. Four things: one copy of each reference shared by everyone, the same release for everyone every time, mistakes caught before they cost a run, and a record of where every file came from.

BENEFIT 1 · NO DUPLICATION

One copy, every name

human

GRCh38

GRCh38_p14_ensembl

data/89c2a7e1…/

one physical copy on disk

Ask by any name

Each alias links to the same file, so nobody downloads again for want of a name.

Shared, not copied

Groups on a cluster read one vault instead of keeping private copies in scratch.

Never fetched twice

The preflight reads the vault, so a re-run downloads only what is missing.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

The first benefit is the simplest. If two researchers ask for the human genome, one as GRCh38.p14 and the other as human, they are both sent through links to the same physical file in the vault, rather than each keeping a private copy in their scratch space. Every genome is always reachable as assembly underscore provider, because Ensembl and GENCODE both publish GRCh38.p14 with different contig names, and your aliases are links straight to the digest directory, renamed, so a tool sees human.fa. And because the preflight asks the vault before downloading, the vault itself is the record of what is done. You can lose Nextflow’s work directory, or run on a cluster that never keeps it, and nothing already registered is fetched twice.

BENEFIT 2 · REPRODUCIBILITY

Releases are added, never replaced

A new release is a new tag

When Ensembl moves to 117, the vault gains a 117 tag beside 116. Nothing an analysis used changes.

Pin it, or follow the provider

A release in the request pins it. Leave it blank and each run checks for a newer one.

Sequences carry their identity

Each genome is filed under a digest of its names, lengths and bases: same sequences, same digest.

# always release 116, whatever is newer

refgenie seek human/ensembl_gtf:116

 

# tags on one genome

ensembl_gtf:116

ensembl_gtf:117  default

fasta_txome:116  from 116

fasta_txome:117  from 117

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Second, reproducibility. What the vault holds never changes under you. An unpinned row follows the provider: when Ensembl publishes release 117, that row is fetched again and the vault gains a 117 tag beside 116, and the default tag only ever moves forward. Anything you derived from 116, like the transcriptome, stays tagged 116 and records its parents. If a project needs to stay on one release, put the release in the request and it is pinned. On identity, one honest correction to what I said in May: refgenie’s digest is not a GA4GH refget hash. It is refgenie’s own digest over each record’s name, length and sequence, related to refget but not conforming to it, and it covers the FASTA only. It is a reliable identifier for the sequences in this vault: same sequences, same digest.

BENEFIT 3 · CORRECTNESS

Mistakes stopped before the run

At resolve time

No annotation where none is published, no two rows for one download, no alias on two genomes.

Before a resource is registered

Enough records on the genome’s sequences, none past a sequence’s end, lengths that agree.

Renamed only where it is safe

dbSNP’s RefSeq names become the genome’s own through NCBI’s assembly report.

ERROR: blacklist:hg38 was NOT

registered for GRCh38_p14_ensembl:

- only 0.0% of its 636 records

  are on sequences this genome has

A real refusal: UCSC chr1 names against an Ensembl genome that says 1.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Third, correctness. Three mistakes that used to surface after a multi-gigabyte download, or not at all, are now caught when the request is resolved. Third-party resources, such as ClinVar, the blacklist, the GATK bundle, dbSNP and the VEP cache, are never registered until they have been checked against the genome: are enough of the records on sequences this genome has, does any record lie beyond the end of its chromosome, do the declared lengths agree. The box is a real refusal: the ENCODE blacklist for hg38 asked for on an Ensembl human genome. Its records say chr1, the genome says 1, and without the check it would have silently filtered nothing. dbSNP is published under RefSeq accessions no genome uses, so it is renamed through NCBI’s assembly report, only where the lengths agree, and then put through the same check.

BENEFIT 4 · PROVENANCE

A record for every asset

provenance.json

Source URLs, accession and taxon, SHA-256 of each file, tool versions and a UTC time, for every download.

RO-Crate

The whole vault described: every genome, asset and file, and each download, derivation and fetch.

index.tsv

The vault as a plain table, readable without refgenie, rewritten after every registration.

Which genome, which release, from where, checked how: what a methods section and a data management plan need.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Fourth, provenance. Every download writes a record: the source URLs, the assembly accession and taxon, SHA-256 checksums of each file and of its contents, a summary of the annotation, tool versions and a UTC timestamp. That record lives in the vault beside the asset, reachable by every alias. The whole vault also describes itself as an RO-Crate, RO-Crate 1.1 with the Process Run Crate profile, listing every genome, asset and file and each download, derivation and fetch, so other tools can read it without knowing anything about refdata-flow. And there is a plain index table for anyone who just wants to see what is held. From a data stewardship point of view, this is the part that answers the questions reviewers and funders ask.

BUILT FOR THE UCL CLUSTERS

One profile for the UCL clusters

StepRuns onWhy
Downloadslaunching machineneed outbound network
Preflight, registration, checkslaunching machineedit the vault’s single config
Transcriptomecompute node1 core · 4 GB · 2 h
Small derived filescompute node1 core · 6 to 8 GB · 2 h

bash run_pipeline.sh requests/requests_raw.csv --profile sge

Myriad, Kathleen and Young; same scheduler request format as rnaseq-flow. Loads and resolves; not yet run against a real scheduler.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

The SGE profile is set up for the UCL Research Computing clusters, Myriad, Kathleen and Young, and asks the scheduler for things the same way rnaseq-flow does: memory per core rounded up, node-local scratch. It splits the work the way the clusters need. Downloads need outbound network, which compute nodes often lack, so they stay on the machine you launched from. So do the preflight, registration and checks, because they edit the vault’s single config. The derivations need neither, so they go to the queue as small jobs. If your site doesn’t allow downloading on a login node, launch from an interactive session or a transfer node. To be clear about status: the profile has been checked to load and resolve, but it has not yet submitted a job to a real scheduler. That is the next milestone.

FROM ANY JOB

Point a job at the vault

# once, or in a shared module file

export REFGENIE=<vault>/refgenie_export.yaml

# what the vault holds, with aliases

refgenie list

# a path any tool can take

refgenie seek human/fasta

# into an nf-core pipeline

nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \

  --fasta $(refgenie seek human/fasta) \

  --gtf $(refgenie seek human/ensembl_gtf)

Paths, not plugins

nf-core pipelines take reference paths as parameters: pass them what refgenie seek prints.

One line for everyone

With Lmod, set REFGENIE in a shared module file and module load brings the vault.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Using the vault from a job is a single environment variable. Set REFGENIE to the vault’s config, once in your profile or, better, in a shared module file, and refgenie list shows every genome with its aliases from any directory. refgenie seek gives you an absolute path you can hand to anything. One correction from May: nf-core pipelines don’t read refgenie themselves. They take reference paths as parameters, so the integration is refgenie seek: one command gives you the path, and you pass it in. With an environment module system like Lmod, a setenv line in a shared module means everyone gets the vault with module load.

THE PROPOSED MODEL

Curated once, read by everyone

01 · CURATED

A service account runs the pipeline to add genomes, resources and databases, then re-applies the lock.

02 · PROTECTED

Owned by the curator and read-only to everyone else, with the directories locked as well as the files.

03 · INHERITED

Hosted in the centre’s read-only reference area, with REFGENIE set in a shared module file.

Requests go to the curator; everyone else only reads. Protection is not backup, so the config is versioned too.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

This is how I’d like it to run on ARC. One curator or service account runs the pipeline to add what people ask for, then re-applies the lock. The vault is owned by that account and read-only to everyone else, and deletion is controlled at the directory, not the file, so the directories are locked too. Ideally it lives in the centre’s curated, read-only reference area with the REFGENIE variable set in a shared module file, so permissions are enforced centrally. Two caveats: the immutable flag isn’t supported on most parallel filesystems, so this rests on ownership and permissions; and permissions prevent edits, not a bad run, so the config should be under version control or snapshots.

refdata-flow · UCL ARC

Where are we? Everything on the left works end to end and is covered by an offline test suite of 321 tests that runs in CI and fails if any test is skipped. The variant resources and databases are the newest part. ClinVar, the yeast VEP cache and Swiss-Prot have been through real runs; the largest, dbSNP and the human VEP cache, are the last to be tried at full size, and dbSNP is held up to three times, about ninety gigabytes, until the work directory is cleaned. Next is deployment on ARC and the first real run through the scheduler. After that I’d like a shared vault to be the default reference for UCL groups, then opt-in aligner indexes, built per tool version, and later a configurable config location.
